books.title: Growth of the Soil
books.author: Knut Hamsun
books.desc: A solitary man clears a farm in the Norwegian wilderness, and with his wife Inger builds a life of patient labour as the modern world approaches.
about: Isak, a strong and simple man, settles on an empty stretch of land in the north of Norway and begins to clear it for farming. He asks passing Lapps to tell women that he needs help, and one day Inger, a sturdy young woman with a harelip, arrives and stays. Together they build the farm of Sellanraa and raise their sons Eleseus and Sivert, helped by the official Geissler and troubled by the scheming Oline. In the second part, the neighbouring settler Axel and the servant Barbro have their own story, as mining, trade and the town reach the wilderness.

Hamsun's novel celebrates the patient work of the soil and the cycle of rural life, and contrasts it with the restlessness of modern society. Its depiction of the Sami, called Lapps in the text, reflects the prejudices of its time.

Growth of the Soil (Markens Grøde) was first published in 1917, and Hamsun was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1920 for this novel. This edition offers the English translation by W. W. Worster and the German translation by Pauline Klaiber.
books.author_short: Norwegian novelist (1859–1952), author of Hunger and Growth of the Soil, winner of the 1920 Nobel Prize in Literature.
author_long: Knut Hamsun was born Knud Pedersen on 4 August 1859 in Lom, in the Gudbrandsdalen valley of Norway. He first became famous with the novel Hunger (1890), and in 1920 received the Nobel Prize in Literature for Growth of the Soil. He died on 19 February 1952.

His works include Hunger (1890), Mysteries (1892), Pan (1894), Victoria (1898) and Growth of the Soil (1917). He openly supported Nazi Germany and the Quisling regime during the German occupation of Norway, and was charged with treason after the war.

books.title: Niels Lyhne
books.author: J. P. Jacobsen
books.desc: A dreamy young Dane who has lost his faith searches for love and for meaning as an artist, and must face death without religion.
about: Niels Lyhne grows up on the estate of Lönborggaard, between a romantic, poetic mother, Bartholine, and a practical father. As a boy he loses his faith in God after the death of his beloved aunt Edele, and later, in Copenhagen, he dreams of becoming a poet. He falls in love with the married Mrs Boye, then with Fennimore, the wife of his friend the painter Erik, and later marries the young Gerda, while trying to live by his convictions as an atheist.

Jacobsen's novel, written in a refined and poetic style, is a work of Scandinavian naturalism that follows a man's failures as a lover and an artist, and is at the same time a critique of atheism and of faith. The poet Rainer Maria Rilke recommended it, with the Bible, as one of the two books most worth reading.
Niels Lyhne was published in 1880. This English translation by Hanna Astrup Larsen appeared in the series Scandinavian Classics.
books.author_short: Danish novelist, poet and scientist (1847–1885), author of Marie Grubbe and Niels Lyhne.
author_long: Jens Peter Jacobsen was born on 7 April 1847 in Thisted, in Jutland, the son of a prosperous merchant. Fascinated by the work of Charles Darwin, he translated The Origin of Species and The Descent of Man into Danish. Struck by tuberculosis while still young, he died of it on 30 April 1885.
Under the influence of the critic Georg Brandes he wrote the historical novel Marie Grubbe (1876), followed by Niels Lyhne (1880). His works also include the story Mogens (1872) and poems.

books.title: Doña Perfecta
books.author: Benito Pérez Galdós
books.desc: A young liberal engineer arrives in a cathedral town to marry his cousin, and meets the hostility of his pious aunt and the local clergy.
about: Don José (Pepe) Rey, a young engineer from Madrid with modern, liberal ideas, travels to the cathedral town of Orbajosa to marry his cousin Rosario, a match arranged between his father and his father's sister, Doña Perfecta. Pepe and Rosario soon fall in love, but the canon of the cathedral, Don Inocencio, and the townspeople, among them the rough Caballuco, distrust the newcomer. When Doña Perfecta learns that Pepe is not a believer, she sets herself against the marriage.

Galdós's realist novel is a powerful study of religious intolerance and fanaticism, and of the conflict between the traditional outlook of the Spanish provinces and the modern, liberal outlook of Madrid.
Doña Perfecta was published in 1876. This English translation is by Mary J. Serrano.
books.author_short: Spanish realist novelist and politician (1843–1920), author of the Episodios Nacionales, Doña Perfecta and Fortunata and Jacinta.
author_long: Benito Pérez Galdós was born on 10 May 1843 in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, the youngest son of an army officer. He became the leading Spanish realist novelist of his century, and in 1914 was elected deputy for Las Palmas. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1912, but his opposition to religious authorities made him enemies among conservative Catholics. He died on 4 January 1920.

Besides his novels of contemporary society, such as Doña Perfecta (1876), he wrote the Episodios Nacionales, a long series of historical novels on Spanish history beginning with the battle of Trafalgar in 1805.

books.title: The Book of Tea
books.author: Okakura Kakuzō
books.desc: Through the Japanese tea ceremony, Okakura explains Zen, Taoism and an art of living based on simplicity and harmony to Western readers.
about: In seven short chapters, Okakura traces the history of tea from a medicine in ancient China to the ritual of the Japanese tea ceremony, which he calls "Teaism". He discusses the schools of tea, Taoism and Zen, the tea room, art appreciation, flowers and the great tea masters, ending with the death of the tea master Rikiu (Sen no Rikyu).

Addressed to a Western audience and written in English, the book links the tea ceremony to Japanese aesthetics and ways of life, praising simplicity, purity and humility, and protests against Western caricatures of "the East".
The Book of Tea was published in 1906, in the wake of the Russo-Japanese War.
books.author_short: Japanese scholar and art critic (1863–1913), author of The Book of Tea.
author_long: Okakura Kakuzō, also known as Okakura Tenshin, was born on 14 February 1863 and learned English at an early age. He studied in Tokyo under the art historian Ernest Fenollosa and became a leading defender of traditional Japanese art and culture in the Meiji era. He died on 2 September 1913.
Outside Japan he is best known for The Book of Tea (1906), written in English.

books.title: Billy Budd and Other Prose Pieces
books.author: Herman Melville
books.desc: In 1797, an innocent and popular young sailor on a British warship is falsely accused of mutiny by the master-at-arms.
about: Billy Budd, a handsome and good-natured young sailor, is pressed into service in 1797 from the merchant ship Rights-of-Man onto a British man-of-war, at a time when the Royal Navy has just been shaken by the mutinies at Spithead and the Nore. Admired by the crew, he arouses the envy of the master-at-arms, John Claggart, who falsely accuses him before Captain Edward Fairfax Vere of plotting mutiny. Unable to answer because of his stammer, Billy strikes his accuser.

Melville's novella is a tragedy of innocence and evil, law and conscience. The volume also contains other prose pieces by Melville, including the essay "Hawthorne and His Mosses" and stories such as "Cock-a-Doodle-Doo!" and "The Paradise of Bachelors and the Tartarus of Maids".

Billy Budd was left unfinished at Melville's death in 1891 and first published in 1924 in this edition by Raymond Weaver, as volume XIII of the Standard Edition of Melville's works. Later editions corrected Weaver's text; in this version the warship is called the Indomitable, renamed Bellipotent in later editions.
